newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Fokker deal nears; suppliers say they'll wait.
newsitem.headline: Fokker deal nears; suppliers say they'll wait.

text.p: The much-heralded deal to rescue bankrupt Dutch planemaker Fokker appeared to edge closer Friday as South Korea's Samsung confirmed it was studying a takeover proposal and key suppliers offered a few more days' breathing space.

Samsung said it was "favorably" reviewing a Dutch government proposal that called for a long-term investment of between $500 million and $600 million but said a deal still lay tantalizingly out of reach.
"We are undertaking negotiations with the Dutch government in a very amicable, positive manner but no agreement has been reached yet," a spokesman for the company said in Seoul.
The Dutch government said it had no comment on the proposal or on the status of negotiations on the future of Fokker -- one of the most esteemed names in the history of flight.
Founded in 1919 by aviation pioneer Anthony Fokker, down the years it has developed some 125 different aircraft, ranging from passenger planes to fighters and bombers.

Fokker's administrators had imposed an end-of-the month deadline for the talks to succeed but on Friday the planemakers' suppliers seemed to offer an olive branch, informing the court appointed receivers they could wait just a few more days.
"Without having formally made new agreements, the (court appointed) administrators have the impression that a few more days of delay should not be insurmountable," the receivers said.
In a statement, the receivers said talks were held on Thursday with Shorts, a Northern Irish unit of Canada's Bombardier, Daimler Benz Aerospace, Airbus GmbH and Rolls Royce, all suppliers to Fokker.
Dutch news agency ANP had quoted a Samsung representative as saying the takeover was a done deal.
"The deal can't go wrong anymore, the only thing to be decided is when it will be announced by Samsung," the agency quoted the representative as saying.
Samsung Aerospace Industries, a unit of the giant Samsung group, wants to make use of Fokker's know-how to build a new generation of regional jets.

The administrators, who have been running Fokker since it was declared bankrupt in March, gave Samsung the exclusive right to examine Fokker's books in September with a view to a possible bid for its core plane-making business.

Samsung sees a resurrected Fokker as a potential shortcut to its ambitions of becoming a major player in the global aerospace industry, but it is unwilling to assume all the risks and has sought substantial investment by the Dutch government.

The government has indicated it is willing to provide fresh capital for Fokker and invest in the development of a new 125-seat regional jet, but Samsung is said to have balked at its demands for long-term job guarantees in the Netherlands.
Since March the administrators have kept the company running with a skeleton staff of 650 people.
